key_insight: Open-source deep learning models for MRI-visible perivascular space segmentation can look accurate internally yet fail to generalize or preserve biologically meaningful associations in Alzheimer’s disease cohorts.
clinical_relevance: For biomarker research and future clinical use, model choice and cohort-specific validation matter because segmentation performance alone may not predict whether downstream disease associations remain valid.
method: Benchmarked five open-source nnU-Net-based PVS segmentation models against manual labels.
Tested performance in 60 multi-site ADNI-3 participants and 12 external VALDO challenge scans.
Compared overall, voxel, object, and lesion-wise Dice and evaluated preservation of PVS-amyloid associations.
evidence_signal: ADNI-PVS-Net had the best internal Dice (0.58±0.14) but dropped to ≤0.11 externally, while MedNet-PVS and mcPVS-Net generalized better (Dice 0.27–0.30) yet often misestimated PVS burden and only AD-trained models reproduced the expected PVS-amyloid relationship.
watch_item: High Dice scores did not guarantee valid biomarker inference, and some models misclassified up to 32% of white matter hyperintensities as PVS.
paper_title: Examining the Clinical Utility of Deep Learning Models for Perivascular Space Segmentation in Alzheimer's Disease
